newsitem.title: UK: UK unemployment falls less than expected in May.
newsitem.headline: UK unemployment falls less than expected in May.

text.p: Unemployment in Britain fell to its lowest level in almost seven years in May but the decline was smaller than expected because of the end of distortions caused by changes to benefit rules.

The Office for National Statistics said Wednesday that the number of people out of work fell by 18,400 to 1.64 million in May, an unemployment rate of 5.8 percent. This compared with 5.9 percent in April and was the lowest rate since September 1990.
Average earnings growth was steady at 4.5 percent in the year to April, indicating no increase in inflationary wage pressures despite the tightening labour market.

The new Labour government welcomed the decline in unemployment, although it said the figures should be treated with caution. It has ordered a review of the way the figures are calculated after accusing the previous Conservative government of "fiddling" them for political reasons.

"The figures are ... consistent with a broad picture of rising output, growth in employment and falling unemployment," education and employment minister Andrew Smith said. "These figures are the first unaffected by distortions to the claimant count caused by the introduction of the Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA)."

The jobseekers' allowance is paid to people who meet new strict criteria for demonstrating that they are actively seeking work. But thousands of people who would like work but cannot find it are not eligible and are therefore not registered as unemployed.
Most economists had expected unemployment to fall by around 40,000 in May after a drop of 56,400 in April.

"The modest drop in unemployment last month may give a truer picture of labour market activity than the declines of 50,000 to 60,000 seen earlier this year," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
He said the unemployment and earnings data would reduce pressure on the Bank of England, newly empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, to tighten monetary policy further.
